text: I The Industrial Revolution and the New Economic History JOEL Moxyr!
text_raw:
I 
The Industrial Revolution and 
the New Economic History 
JOEL Moxyr!

text: Almost a century has passed since the publication of Arnold Toynbee’s famous Lec- tures on the Industrial Revolution (1884).
text_raw:
Almost a century has passed since the publication of Arnold Toynbee’s famous Lec- 
tures on the Industrial Revolution (1884).

text: Historians of all persuasions have since come to the conclusion that the Industrial Revolution in Britain constituted a new point of departure in human history, an event of such moment to daily life that it compares to the advent of monotheism or the development of language.
text_raw:
Historians of all persuasions have since 
come to the conclusion that the Industrial Revolution in Britain constituted a new 
point of departure in human history, an event of such moment to daily life that it 
compares to the advent of monotheism or the development of language.

text: Conse- quently, a vast literature has emerged dealing with its various aspects, written by his- torians, economists, and sociologists, both left wing and right wing, English and foreign.
text_raw:
Conse- 
quently, a vast literature has emerged dealing with its various aspects, written by his- 
torians, economists, and sociologists, both left wing and right wing, English and 
foreign.

text: Little agreement has emerged among the experts about the fundamental questions.
text_raw:
Little agreement has emerged among the experts about the fundamental 
questions.

text: There is, first, the mere question of definition: what exactly was the Indus- trial Revolution? ?
text_raw:
There is, first, the mere question of definition: what exactly was the Indus- 
trial Revolution? ?

text: Of the many attempts to sum up what the Industrial Revolution meant, Perkin’s is perhaps the most eloquent.
text_raw:
Of the many attempts to sum up what the Industrial Revolution 
meant, Perkin’s is perhaps the most eloquent.

text: In his words, it was “a revolution in men’s access to the means of life, in control of their ecological environment, in their capacity to escape from the tyranny and niggardliness of nature... it opened the road for men to complete mastery of their physical environment, without the inesca- pable need to exploit each other” (Perkin, 1969, pp.
text_raw:
In his words, it was “a revolution in 
men’s access to the means of life, in control of their ecological environment, in their 
capacity to escape from the tyranny and niggardliness of nature... it opened the 
road for men to complete mastery of their physical environment, without the inesca- 
pable need to exploit each other” (Perkin, 1969, pp.

text: More changed in Britain than just the way in which goods and services were produced.
text_raw:
More changed in Britain 
than just the way in which goods and services were produced.

text: The nature of family and household, the status of women and children, the role of the church, how people chose their rulers and supported their poor, what they knew about the world and what they wanted to know—all of these were transformed.
text_raw:
The nature of family 
and household, the status of women and children, the role of the church, how people 
chose their rulers and supported their poor, what they knew about the world and 
what they wanted to know—all of these were transformed.

text: It is a continuing project to discover how these noneconomic changes affected and were affected by economic change.
text_raw:
It is a continuing project 
to discover how these noneconomic changes affected and were affected by economic 
change.

text: The Revolution was, in Perkin’s irresistible phrase, a “more than industrial revolution.” By focusing on economics we isolate only a part, though a central part, of the modernization of Britain.
text_raw:
The Revolution was, in Perkin’s irresistible phrase, a “more than industrial 
revolution.” By focusing on economics we isolate only a part, though a central part, 
of the modernization of Britain.

text: Difficult and ambitious questions have been posed.
text_raw: Difficult and ambitious questions have been posed.

text: What were the causes of the Industrial Revolution?
text_raw:
What were the causes of the 
Industrial Revolution?

text: Why did it occur when it did?
text_raw: Why did it occur when it did?

text: What were the effects on the economic and social welfare of the population?
text_raw:
What were the effects on the 
economic and social welfare of the population?

text: What were the roles played by agri-
text_raw: What were the roles played by agri-

text: 2 THEECONOMICS OF THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION culture, population growth, political elements, transportation, and foreign trade?
text_raw:
2 THEECONOMICS OF THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION 
culture, population growth, political elements, transportation, and foreign trade?

text: No consensus had emerged on any of these questions by the early 1960s.* Those who seek definitive answers should not venture into economic history.
text_raw:
No 
consensus had emerged on any of these questions by the early 1960s.* Those who seek 
definitive answers should not venture into economic history.

text: The inherent impor- tance of the subject matter, however, has kept scholars and students interested and the literature dealing with the Industrial Revolution has grown extensively in the last decade.
text_raw:
The inherent impor- 
tance of the subject matter, however, has kept scholars and students interested and 
the literature dealing with the Industrial Revolution has grown extensively in the last 
decade.

text: The topic has attracted many lively controversies.
text_raw: The topic has attracted many lively controversies.

text: This tendency to generate debates is no drawback; the mortal enemy of economic history is not error but bore- dom.
text_raw:
This tendency to generate 
debates is no drawback; the mortal enemy of economic history is not error but bore- 
dom.

text: As long as the subject can generate vigorous discussions among some of the finest minds working in economics and history departments, it should consider itself alive and well.
text_raw:
As long as the subject can generate vigorous discussions among some of the 
finest minds working in economics and history departments, it should consider itself 
alive and well.

text: In the past two decades, economists have played an increasing role in the historio- graphy of the Industrial Revolution.
text_raw:
In the past two decades, economists have played an increasing role in the historio- 
graphy of the Industrial Revolution.

text: A New Economic History, eager to apply its tools to new subjects, looked on the Industrial Revolution as an easy target of scholarship.
text_raw:
A New Economic History, eager to apply its tools 
to new subjects, looked on the Industrial Revolution as an easy target of scholarship.

text: Some scholars indeed have expressed the hope that economic analysis and quan- titative models would resolve some of the controversies (Hartwell, 1971, pp.
text_raw:
Some scholars indeed have expressed the hope that economic analysis and quan- 
titative models would resolve some of the controversies (Hartwell, 1971, pp.

text: The articles reprinted in this volume contain a sampling of the work of economists and economic historians familiar with economic analysis on subjects related to the Industrial Revolution.
text_raw:
The articles reprinted in this volume contain a sampling of the work of 
economists and economic historians familiar with economic analysis on subjects 
related to the Industrial Revolution.

text: It should be pointed out that this collection does not pretend to be a systematic “New Economic History of the Industrial Revolution.” It is not a complete coverage of the subject, but it addresses a number of important and well-defined aspects of it.
text_raw:
It should be pointed out that this collection does 
not pretend to be a systematic “New Economic History of the Industrial Revolution.” 
It is not a complete coverage of the subject, but it addresses a number of important 
and well-defined aspects of it.

text: The New Economic History has shown itself best quali- fied to answer questions that it itself poses, often well-defined questions that yielded clear, refutable hypotheses.
text_raw:
The New Economic History has shown itself best quali- 
fied to answer questions that it itself poses, often well-defined questions that yielded 
clear, refutable hypotheses.

text: Indeed, the very definiteness of the new methods has con- fined them to a narrow range of problems.
text_raw:
Indeed, the very definiteness of the new methods has con- 
fined them to a narrow range of problems.

text: An important contribution of economists has been a more sophisticated and ima- ginative use of statistics to test hypotheses about causal relations in the Industrial Revolution.® The New Economic History has used existing statistics in new and ima- ginative ways and has added significantly to the body of quantitative information concerning England during the Industrial Revolution.® But most important, the New Economic History has imposed certain standards of economic logic upon the field.
text_raw:
An important contribution of economists has been a more sophisticated and ima- 
ginative use of statistics to test hypotheses about causal relations in the Industrial 
Revolution.® The New Economic History has used existing statistics in new and ima- 
ginative ways and has added significantly to the body of quantitative information 
concerning England during the Industrial Revolution.® But most important, the New 
Economic History has imposed certain standards of economic logic upon the field.

text: Economists are not less prejudiced and politically biased than other social scientists, and they certainly do not monopolize common sense (the strong beliefs of some members of the profession notwithstanding).
text_raw:
Economists are not less prejudiced and politically biased than other social scientists, 
and they certainly do not monopolize common sense (the strong beliefs of some 
members of the profession notwithstanding).

text: But economics allows at least fewer logi- cal lapses than other social sciences and when an economist commits them, he or she can count on other economists to point them out mercilessly.’ Although disputes con- tinue, they are fought with sharper and more accurate tools than before.
text_raw:
But economics allows at least fewer logi- 
cal lapses than other social sciences and when an economist commits them, he or she 
can count on other economists to point them out mercilessly.’ Although disputes con- 
tinue, they are fought with sharper and more accurate tools than before.

text: Arguments can be—at least in principle—proven wrong.

text: A Survey DONALD McCLOSKEY The Quiet Revolution and Its Historians In the 80 years or so after 1780 the population of Britain nearly tripled, the towns of Liverpool and Manchester became gigantic cities, the average income of the popula- tion more than doubled, the share of farming fell from just under half to just under one-fifth of the nation’s output, and the making of textiles and iron moved into steam-driven factories.
text_raw:
A Survey 
DONALD McCLOSKEY 
The Quiet Revolution and Its Historians 
In the 80 years or so after 1780 the population of Britain nearly tripled, the towns of 
Liverpool and Manchester became gigantic cities, the average income of the popula- 
tion more than doubled, the share of farming fell from just under half to just under 
one-fifth of the nation’s output, and the making of textiles and iron moved into 
steam-driven factories.

text: So strange were these events that before they happened they were not anticipated and while they were happening they were not comprehended.
text_raw:
So strange were these events that before they happened they 
were not anticipated and while they were happening they were not comprehended.

text: In 1700 a percipient observer of Britain looking towards 1780 might have anticipated its enlarged foreign trade and more active workshops (as, in fact, Daniel Defoe had); in 1860 he might have anticipated the competition of new industrial nations or the application of science to factory and farm during the half-century to come, and by 1900 he would at least have comprehended these events happening (as, in fact, the economist Alfred Marshall and others did).
text_raw:
In 1700 a percipient observer of Britain looking towards 1780 might have anticipated 
its enlarged foreign trade and more active workshops (as, in fact, Daniel Defoe had); 
in 1860 he might have anticipated the competition of new industrial nations or the 
application of science to factory and farm during the half-century to come, and by 
1900 he would at least have comprehended these events happening (as, in fact, the 
economist Alfred Marshall and others did).

text: Yet in 1776 Adam Smith predicted a Bri- tain of merchants, farmers, and artificers increasing their incomes at a moderate pace through specialization and trade—after which national income increased in eight decades by a factor of nearly seven.

would swallow whatever the increase would bring—after which rents as a share of 
national income fell, 1801 to 1861, from about 17 percent to about 8 percent.

text: And in 1848 Karl Marx, in the midst of economic events belying his prediction, predicted that monopoly capital would swallow all—after which the share of labor in income rose, and the real wages of the exploited classes increased in ten or fifteen years by some 15 percent and in fifty years by 80 percent.

text: SOLOW and PETER TEMIN The purpose of this essay is to advance our understanding of industrial develop- ment by describing the progress what economists call the “factors of production,” i.e., the inputs out of which food, clothing, and shelter are made.
text_raw:
SOLOW and 
PETER TEMIN 
The purpose of this essay is to advance our understanding of industrial develop- 
ment by describing the progress what economists call the “factors of production,” 
i.e., the inputs out of which food, clothing, and shelter are made.

text: It is by no means clear, however, that the increase in our ability to produce food, clothing, and shelter that we call “the industrial revolution” was a direct result of an increase in the fac- tors of production.
text_raw:
It is by no means 
clear, however, that the increase in our ability to produce food, clothing, and shelter 
that we call “the industrial revolution” was a direct result of an increase in the fac- 
tors of production.

text: In fact, the relation between the traditional factors of production—land, labor, and capital—and the ability of an economy to produce is far more complex than the use of the words “inputs” and “outputs” might suggest.
text_raw:
In fact, the relation between the traditional factors of 
production—land, labor, and capital—and the ability of an economy to produce is far 
more complex than the use of the words “inputs” and “outputs” might suggest.

text: We therefore introduce the discussion of the factors of production by an attempt to set forward the relations between these factors and industrial development that is the subject of this book.
text_raw:
We 
therefore introduce the discussion of the factors of production by an attempt to set 
forward the relations between these factors and industrial development that is the 
subject of this book.

text: It is a great abstraction to talk of the economy as a whole and of only a few factors of production.
text_raw:
It is a great abstraction to talk of the economy as a whole and of only a few factors 
of production.

text: The uses of such an abstraction are obvious: it enables us to make gen- eralizations, to compare countries with each other,and to direct our research into areas of potential usefulness.
text_raw:
The uses of such an abstraction are obvious: it enables us to make gen-

text: 182 THEECONOMICS OF THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION For clergy and schoolmasters, we have made use of private pay series.
text_raw:
182 THEECONOMICS OF THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION 
For clergy and schoolmasters, we have made use of private pay series.

text: Clergymen’s mean annual earnings (including the rental value of the vicarage) can be estimated for the greater part of the nineteenth century by using The Clerical Guide and Ecclesiastical Directory and The Clergy List.
text_raw:
Clergymen’s 
mean annual earnings (including the rental value of the vicarage) can be estimated 
for the greater part of the nineteenth century by using The Clerical Guide and 
Ecclesiastical Directory and The Clergy List.

text: A random sample of 550 clergymen, from all patronage sources (royal, ecclesiastical, university, and private) yields their pay for 1827, 1835, and 1851.
text_raw:
A random sample of 550 clergymen, 
from all patronage sources (royal, ecclesiastical, university, and private) yields their 
pay for 1827, 1835, and 1851.

text: For earlier benchmark years we had to use public pay rates for clergy, splicing these on to the private series at 1827.
text_raw:
For earlier benchmark years we had to use public pay 
rates for clergy, splicing these on to the private series at 1827.

text: This procedure seems to have yielded plausible pay series for the average clergyman back to 1755, judging by the similarity in trend between public and private clergy salaries from 1827 on.
text_raw:
This procedure seems 
to have yielded plausible pay series for the average clergyman back to 1755, judging 
by the similarity in trend between public and private clergy salaries from 1827 on.

text: Schoolmasters had low monthly cash earnings, both because much of their income was in kind (rents and fuel), and because they often received supplementary fees and holiday bonuses.
text_raw:
Schoolmasters had low monthly cash earnings, both because much of their income 
was in kind (rents and fuel), and because they often received supplementary fees and 
holiday bonuses.

text: We have assumed that income in kind was a stable share of total income, so that the twelve-month cash-income series in Table 9.2 accurately reflects trends in total income.
text_raw:
We have assumed that income in kind was a stable share of total 
income, so that the twelve-month cash-income series in Table 9.2 accurately reflects 
trends in total income.

text: For 1755—1835, our estimates rely on schoolmasters’ earnings in several Charity Schools in Staffordshire and Warwickshire.
text_raw:
For 1755—1835, our estimates rely on schoolmasters’ earnings 
in several Charity Schools in Staffordshire and Warwickshire.

text: The 1851 figure refers to civilian schoolmasters in public pay, as reported in the Annual Estimates.” For nineteenth-century manufacturing and building crafts (Series 2H to 6H inclusive), the well-known estimates of Bowley and Wood suffice.’ The available series on eighteenth-century artisans’ pay refer only to the building crafts, but Gilboy’s data on these crafts offer the advantage of regional diversity.
text_raw:
The 1851 figure refers 
to civilian schoolmasters in public pay, as reported in the Annual Estimates.” 
For nineteenth-century manufacturing and building crafts (Series 2H to 6H 
inclusive), the well-known estimates of Bowley and Wood suffice.’ The available 
series on eighteenth-century artisans’ pay refer only to the building crafts, but 
Gilboy’s data on these crafts offer the advantage of regional diversity.

text: To give proper weight to the well-known regional variance in nominal wages, and to the shift in eighteenth-century populations, we have constructed an earnings average for build- ing craftsmen that reflects changes in the “regional mix” between 1755 and 1797.4 The result is a steeper rise in earnings in the building trades up to 1797 than that reported by Brown and Hopkins, whose series referred to southern England only (Phelps Brown and Hopkins, 1955, pp.
text_raw:
To give proper 
weight to the well-known regional variance in nominal wages, and to the shift in 
eighteenth-century populations, we have constructed an earnings average for build- 
ing craftsmen that reflects changes in the “regional mix” between 1755 and 1797.4 
The result is a steeper rise in earnings in the building trades up to 1797 than that 
reported by Brown and Hopkins, whose series referred to southern England only 
(Phelps Brown and Hopkins, 1955, pp.

text: Three very large unskilled occupations remain: colliers, non-farm common labor- ers, and farm laborers.
text_raw:
Three very large unskilled occupations remain: colliers, non-farm common labor- 
ers, and farm laborers.

text: The colliers’ earnings figures refer to underground mining by adult males.
text_raw:
The colliers’ earnings figures refer to underground mining by 
adult males.

text: The 1851 figure is derived from Wood’s wage series.'° The 1835 figure is from Bowley, as are the 1810-19 estimates, the latter referring to southern Scotland.
text_raw:
The 1851 figure is derived from Wood’s wage series.'° The 1835 figure is 
from Bowley, as are the 1810-19 estimates, the latter referring to southern Scotland.

text: We have also used figures for 1755 to 1805 inclusive, and (again) 1835 from Ashton and Sykes, referring to colliers’ daily wage rates in the northern counties, in Lan- cashire and Derbyshire (Bowley, 1900;
Ashton and Sykes, 1929).
text_raw: Ashton and Sykes, 1929).

text: These diverse esti- mates are linked together at various dates and converted into annual earnings rates using the procedures sketched above.
text_raw:
These diverse esti- 
mates are linked together at various dates and converted into annual earnings rates 
using the procedures sketched above.

text: Non-farm common laborers’ earnings are based on two sources.
text_raw:
Non-farm common laborers’ earnings are based 
on two sources.

text: For the period 1797-1851, we have accepted the Phelps Brown- Hopkins estimates for laborers in the building trades.
text_raw:
For the period 1797-1851, we have accepted the Phelps Brown- 
Hopkins estimates for laborers in the building trades.

text: For 1755-97, their estimates have been set aside in favor of a multi-regional series based on Gilboy data for build- ing labor, using the same procedure described for building crafts above.
text_raw:
For 1755-97, their estimates 
have been set aside in favor of a multi-regional series based on Gilboy data for build- 
ing labor, using the same procedure described for building crafts above.

text: For farm laborers, the 1797-1851 figures are based on Bowley’s wages for a “normal work week”, taking account of both income in kind and seasonal wage-rate variation (but not seasonal employment variation).'° Fifty-two “normal weeks” are arbitrarily assumed in constructing an annual full-time series.
text_raw:
For farm 
laborers, the 1797-1851 figures are based on Bowley’s wages for a “normal work 
week”, taking account of both income in kind and seasonal wage-rate variation (but 
not seasonal employment variation).'° Fifty-two “normal weeks” are arbitrarily 
assumed in constructing an annual full-time series.

text: The 1781 figure also relies on Bowley, but here it is an unweighted average of the figures for Surrey, Kent, Hert- fordshire, Suffolk, Cumberland, and Monmouth, spliced to the national series at 1797.
text_raw:
The 1781 figure also relies on 
Bowley, but here it is an unweighted average of the figures for Surrey, Kent, Hert- 
fordshire, Suffolk, Cumberland, and Monmouth, spliced to the national series at 1797.

text: The 1755—81 estimates are constructed from raw earnings data collected by Rogers.'”
text_raw: The 1755—81 estimates are constructed from raw earnings data collected by Rogers.'”

text_raw:

text: The variety is striking.
text_raw: The variety is striking.

text: In the latter half of the eighteenth century, farm and non-farm common laborers gained ground on higher-paid workers, the labor aristocracy especially.
text_raw:
In the latter half of the eighteenth century, 
farm and non-farm common laborers gained ground on higher-paid workers, the labor

text: From 1815 to the middle of the nineteenth century, on the other hand, the gap between higher- and lower-paid workers widened dramatically.
text_raw:
From 1815 to the middle of the nineteenth century, on the 
other hand, the gap between higher- and lower-paid workers widened dramatically.

text: Farm wages sagged below, while white-collar pay soared above, the wages for all other groups.'?
text_raw:
Farm wages sagged below, while white-collar pay soared above, the wages for all 
other groups.'?

text: Table 9.3 also compares our results with earlier series that have shaped past impressions of wage trends and played a key role in Flinn’s recent survey (Flinn, 1974).
text_raw:
Table 9.3 also compares our results with earlier series that have 
shaped past impressions of wage trends and played a key role in Flinn’s recent survey

text: The new and old series exhibit both conformity and contrast.
text_raw: The new and old series exhibit both conformity and contrast.

ENGLISH WORKERS’ LIVING STANDARDS 185 
The commodities included in the cost-of-living index also need revision.

text: We have added more relevant working-class commodities, especially potatoes.
text_raw:
We have 
added more relevant working-class commodities, especially potatoes.

text: Some irrelevant industrial raw materials, included in the Gayer-Rostow-Schwartz series, have been removed.
text_raw:
Some irrelevant 
industrial raw materials, included in the Gayer-Rostow-Schwartz series, have been 
removed.

text: But the most important change is the addition of house rent.
text_raw: But the most important change is the addition of house rent.

text: While the classic indices all omitted this important part of the cost-of-living,” ours includes a rent series based on a few dozen cottages in Trentham, Staffordshire (just outside Stoke-on-Trent).
text_raw:
While the 
classic indices all omitted this important part of the cost-of-living,” ours includes a 
rent series based on a few dozen cottages in Trentham, Staffordshire (just outside 
Stoke-on-Trent).

text: While the data base is narrow, it does apply to a housing stock of almost unchanging quality.” The rent series implies that the cost of housing (at a fixed location) rose relative to other consumer items throughout the Industrial Revo- lution, thus offering some new support to the pessimists.” Finally, the cost-of-living index should use commodity weights which reflect work- ers’ budgets shares.
text_raw:
While the data base is narrow, it does apply to a housing stock of 
almost unchanging quality.” The rent series implies that the cost of housing (at a 
fixed location) rose relative to other consumer items throughout the Industrial Revo- 
lution, thus offering some new support to the pessimists.” 
Finally, the cost-of-living index should use commodity weights which reflect work- 
ers’ budgets shares.

text: Past series do not fully satisfy this requirement.
text_raw: Past series do not fully satisfy this requirement.

text: All exclude any weight for housing, some include industrial inputs, and others are simply vague about their weights.
text_raw:
All exclude any 
weight for housing, some include industrial inputs, and others are simply vague about 
their weights.

text: One set of workers’ household budgets stems from the pioneering work of Davies and Eden on the rural poor in the late eighteenth century.” Another is a miscellaneous group of urban workers’ budgets from the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.”° The urban workers’ budgets reveal a lower share spent on food, and a higher share spent on housing, than do the rural poor studied by Davies and Eden.
text_raw:
One set of workers’ household budgets stems from the pioneering work 
of Davies and Eden on the rural poor in the late eighteenth century.” Another is a 
miscellaneous group of urban workers’ budgets from the late eighteenth and early 
nineteenth centuries.”° The urban workers’ budgets reveal a lower share spent on 
food, and a higher share spent on housing, than do the rural poor studied by Davies 
and Eden.

text: Choosing the most appropriate set of budget weights could matter a great deal.
text_raw: Choosing the most appropriate set of budget weights could matter a great deal.

text: Goods and services are consumed in different proportions by northern and southern households, by the rural and the urban, or by the poor and rich.
text_raw:
Goods and services are consumed in different proportions by northern and southern 
households, by the rural and the urban, or by the poor and rich.

text: Cost of living trends could differ across classes simply because of differences in budget weights, as hap- pened often in American experience (Williamson, 1976;
Williamson and Lindert, 1980, chap.
text_raw:
Williamson and Lindert, 
1980, chap.

text: This possibility was pursued with four separate cost-of-living indices using weights from the rural north, rural south, urban north, and urban south.
text_raw:
This possibility was pursued with four separate cost-of-living indices 
using weights from the rural north, rural south, urban north, and urban south.

text: As it happens, prices moved in such a way that the choice of weights mattered very little.
text_raw:
As it 
happens, prices moved in such a way that the choice of weights mattered very little.

text: The reason is that the net rise in the price of food relative to manufactures, which would have impoverished the rural poor more than the better-paid urban workers, was offset by the equally impressive relative rise in house rents, which took a greater toll on urban households.
text_raw:
The reason is that the net rise in the price of food relative to manufactures, which 
would have impoverished the rural poor more than the better-paid urban workers, 
was offset by the equally impressive relative rise in house rents, which took a greater

text: The analysis below continues to use southern urban weights, but we now know that the choice makes little difference.

weights, but we now know that the choice makes little difference.

V 
Time and again the unemployment issue has brought discussion of trends in workers’ 
living standards to a halt: lacking national unemployment data before 1851, how can 
the real wage series be trusted as indicators of annual earnings?

text: Into this empirical vacuum Hobsbawm has injected fragmentary hints about unemployment in the indus- trial north, suggesting that the depression of 1841—43 was “almost certainly the worst of the century.” Yet no conceivable level of unemployment could have cancelled the near-doubling of full-time wages and left the workers of the 1840s with less than their grandfathers had had.
text_raw:
Into this empirical 
vacuum Hobsbawm has injected fragmentary hints about unemployment in the indus- 
trial north, suggesting that the depression of 1841—43 was “almost certainly the worst 
of the century.” 
Yet no conceivable level of unemployment could have cancelled the near-doubling 
of full-time wages and left the workers of the 1840s with less than their grandfathers 
had had.

text: Such a cancellation of gains would require that the national unemployment rate would have had to rise from zero to 50 per cent, or from 10 per cent to 55 per cent—jumps which even the most ardent pessimist would dismiss as inconceivable.
text_raw:
Such a cancellation of gains would require that the national unemployment 
rate would have had to rise from zero to 50 per cent, or from 10 per cent to 55 per 
cent—jumps which even the most ardent pessimist would dismiss as inconceivable.

text: Even in the 1930s, unemployment was less than a quarter of the labor force.
text_raw: Even in the 1930s, unemployment was less than a quarter of the labor force.

text: The 1840s lacked the availability of unemployment compensation, the sharp drop in out- put, wages and prices, as well as the fall in the investment share that accompanied record jobless rates ninety years later.
text_raw:
The 
1840s lacked the availability of unemployment compensation, the sharp drop in out- 
put, wages and prices, as well as the fall in the investment share that accompanied 
record jobless rates ninety years later.

text: We can be more precise about the extent to which the unemployment issue has been overstated in the standard of living debate.
text_raw:

been overstated in the standard of living debate.

text: We have a number of clues about early nineteenth-century unemployment in Britain that have yet to be exploited.

early nineteenth-century unemployment in Britain that have yet to be exploited.

text: Let us examine these, focusing on the controversial period 1820—50, beginning with the non-agricultural sector before tackling the knottier problem of agricultural underem- ployment.

us examine these, focusing on the controversial period 1820—50, beginning with the 
non-agricultural sector before tackling the knottier problem of agricultural underem- 
ployment.

text: We can put an upper limit on non-agricultural unemployment in the 1850s by starting with the share of engineering, metal and shipbuilding union membership who were out of work: in 1851, 3.9 per cent were out at any one time, and the average was 5.2 per cent for 1851—59.

text: This conclusion is derived mainly from the data on relative weekly earnings in Table 9.7.

text: Thus, it appears that an employment-weighted average of the wage rates of women and children together would have advanced about as fast as those for adult male farm laborers in the course of the century 1750-1850.

and children together would have advanced about as fast as those for adult male farm 
laborers in the course of the century 1750-1850.

text: This conclusion would not be over- turned by noting the decline in overall labor-force participation of both women and children.** An optimist might interpret this decline as voluntary, that is as showing that the implicit purchasing power (the “shadow price”) of time spent away from work rose faster than the observed wage rates.

text: Since wage rates differ between occupations, migration from low- paid to high- paid employment can raise average wages for the working class as a whole, even if wage rates do not change for any one occupation.

text: To link workers’ early deaths with rising capitalism, Engels drew on several available estimates showing that mortality was worse in the cities than the countryside, appal- ling in Liverpool and Manchester, and worst in the most crowded neighborhoods of the same cities.
text_raw:
To link workers’ early deaths with rising capitalism, Engels drew on several available 
estimates showing that mortality was worse in the cities than the countryside, appal- 
ling in Liverpool and Manchester, and worst in the most crowded neighborhoods of 
the same cities.

text: A host of studies has since confirmed this spatial pattern of mortality.
text_raw: A host of studies has since confirmed this spatial pattern of mortality.

text: Two pitfalls await anyone trying, as Engels did, to infer from such patterns that working-class longevity diminished as the Industrial Revolution progressed.
text_raw:
Two pitfalls await anyone trying, as Engels did, to infer from such patterns that 
working-class longevity diminished as the Industrial Revolution progressed.

text: First, it is important to remember that the working classes were not neatly segregated from the upper classes by place of residence.
text_raw:
First, it is 
important to remember that the working classes were not neatly segregated from the 
upper classes by place of residence.

text: Liverpool was no closer to being purely working- class than was England in the aggregate.
text_raw:
Liverpool was no closer to being purely working- 
class than was England in the aggregate.

text: On the contrary, census figures show that the socio-occupational group most concentrated in the unhealthy cities was the bour- geoisie, although most bought their way out of the worst sections by paying higher rents in the more salubrious sections of the same unhealthy cities.
text_raw:
On the contrary, census figures show that 
the socio-occupational group most concentrated in the unhealthy cities was the bour- 
geoisie, although most bought their way out of the worst sections by paying higher 
rents in the more salubrious sections of the same unhealthy cities.

text: The rise of centres of bad health gives no more support to the pessimists’ view of working-class condi- tions than the nineteenth-century decline in national mortality gives to the optimists’ position.
text_raw:
The rise of centres 
of bad health gives no more support to the pessimists’ view of working-class condi- 
tions than the nineteenth-century decline in national mortality gives to the optimists’ 
position.

text: Thanks to the energies of William Farr and a few other scholars, a fairly clear pic- ture of adult male working-class life expectancy can be put together towards the end of the Industrial Revolution.
text_raw:

ture of adult male working-class life expectancy can be put together towards the end 
of the Industrial Revolution.

text: As we have shown elsewhere, life expectancies did not differ dramatically across occupations for England and Wales as a whole.
text_raw:
As we have shown elsewhere, life expectancies did not 
differ dramatically across occupations for England and Wales as a whole.

text: The occu- pational differences were far smaller than the spatial differences, though the esti- mates may be slightly biased toward uniformity by migration effects and by the omis- sion of paupers from the available figures.*7 We are warned that occupational dif- ferentials were unlikely to have been as great as stark contrasts between Manchester and rural Norfolk would suggest.

text: Past observers have inferred that mortality must have worsened for city-dwellers (and for the working class) since mortality was higher in fast-growing growing cities.

text: Such inferences are unwarranted.
text_raw:
Such inferences are

text: In fact, mortality improved (receded) in the countryside and most cities, and did so by enough to improve national life expectancy from about 1800 on.
text_raw:
In fact, mortality improved (receded) in the countryside and most 
cities, and did so by enough to improve national life expectancy from about 1800 on.

text: The exceptional cities were Liverpool and Manchester, where crude death rates stayed about the same from 1801 to 1851, while age-adjusted death rates appear to have risen only slightly up to 1820 and declined slightly to mid-century.” In short, while we cannot yet determine trends in working-class infant and child mortality, it can be shown that any tendency of the rising industrial centres to lure adult workers to an early death was fully offset, or more than offset, by the lengthen- ing of life both in the cities and the countryside.

The exceptional cities were Liverpool and Manchester, where crude death rates 
stayed about the same from 1801 to 1851, while age-adjusted death rates appear to

text_raw: How is their voice to be heard?

Some pro-

text: Schofield argues that the “long period of stability” in literacy in the eighteenth century suggests that “for England, at least, the usual causal relationship between literacy and economic growth might profitably be reversed.” But taking the conven- tional dates of the first Industrial Revolution to be between 1760 and 1840, and assuming, as Schofield does, that entry into the labor force may be taken to-be fifteen years prior to marriage (i.e. at school leaving), then 1790 is the date when the long- term stability in male literacy changed to one of definite improvement.’ It follows that, despite the unprecedented population growth after 1760, England was not only able to maintain the male literacy rate that had been constant for twenty years preceding the industrial revolution, but well before half the “revolution” period was over, and at a time when the population explosion was in full force, it managed to begin an upward trend.

text: Vv I conclude that the recent attempts to reject Bowman and Anderson’s “threshold theory” of literacy, as it applies to England and Wales, have not been successful; second, that available national estimates do not demonstrate that the Industrial Revo- lution depressed literacy—even if we consider the rate for males or females exclusively; third, that the date of distinct improvement in the national literacy trend coincided with the beginnings of the large-scale factory system; and fourth, that the apparent local exception of Lancashire is closer to the national trend than has been believed, and that in any case when we take Irish immigration into account, the asso- ciation between education and economic growth is considerably strengthened.
text_raw:
Vv 
I conclude that the recent attempts to reject Bowman and Anderson’s “threshold 
theory” of literacy, as it applies to England and Wales, have not been successful; 
second, that available national estimates do not demonstrate that the Industrial Revo- 
lution depressed literacy—even if we consider the rate for males or females 
exclusively; third, that the date of distinct improvement in the national literacy trend 
coincided with the beginnings of the large-scale factory system; and fourth, that the 
apparent local exception of Lancashire is closer to the national trend than has been 
believed, and that in any case when we take Irish immigration into account, the asso- 
ciation between education and economic growth is considerably strengthened.
